name: Remitting Seronegative Symmetrical Synovitis with Pitting Oedema
aliases: Remitting seronegative symmetrical synovitis with pitting oedema (RS3PE)
remitting seronegative symmetrical synovitis with pitting edema

clinicalPearls: Characterised by abrupt-onset, symmetrical polyarthritis of the small joints of the hands and feet accompanied by striking pitting oedema over the dorsum of both hands and feet, classically producing a 'boxing-glove' appearance.
Predominantly affects older adults with a male preponderance, and is by definition seronegative for rheumatoid factor and anti-cyclic citrullinated peptide antibodies.
Inflammatory markers are typically elevated, and imaging with ultrasound or magnetic resonance demonstrates extensor tenosynovitis and subcutaneous oedema rather than aggressive erosive synovitis.
The response to low-dose corticosteroids is characteristically rapid and dramatic, often within days, which supports the diagnosis retrospectively.
The disease is usually self-limiting and non-erosive, distinguishing it from elderly-onset rheumatoid arthritis, with which it overlaps clinically.

A paraneoplastic form exists; atypical features, constitutional upset, poor or short-lived steroid response, or relapse should prompt an age-appropriate search for occult solid-organ or haematological malignancy.
Overlap with polymyalgia rheumatica and late-onset spondyloarthritis is recognised, and some patients later evolve towards a defined connective-tissue or seronegative arthropathy.
Human leucocyte antigen associations have been reported, and elevated serum vascular endothelial growth factor is thought to underlie the prominent oedema.
reference.pathophysiology: The syndrome is understood as a distinctive seronegative inflammatory arthropathy of the ageing musculoskeletal system in which synovitis of the small joints is accompanied by prominent flexor and extensor tenosynovitis, and the characteristic dorsal pitting oedema reflects increased vascular permeability and inflammatory exudation within the peritendinous soft tissues rather than joint effusion alone. Elevated circulating vascular endothelial growth factor has been repeatedly implicated as a driver of the vascular leak and oedema, and matrix metalloproteinases and pro-inflammatory cytokines contribute to the synovial and tenosynovial inflammation. Immunosenescence and a dysregulated innate response in older adults are thought to predispose to the abrupt inflammatory storm, while the frequent association with occult neoplasia in a subset suggests that tumour-derived factors can act as a paraneoplastic trigger of the same final pathway. The predominantly non-erosive, remitting behaviour and exquisite corticosteroid responsiveness distinguish the process pathophysiologically from the persistent, autoantibody-driven and erosive synovitis of rheumatoid arthritis, placing it within a spectrum that also encompasses polymyalgia rheumatica and late-onset spondyloarthritis.
additionalDifferentials: Crystal arthropathy including calcium pyrophosphate deposition and gout
Non-inflammatory causes of limb oedema such as venous, cardiac, renal or lymphatic disease
additionalInvestigations: Rheumatoid factor and anti-cyclic citrullinated peptide antibodies, expected to be negative
Erythrocyte sedimentation rate and C-reactive protein
Full blood count with blood film
Ultrasound or magnetic resonance imaging of the hands and feet to demonstrate tenosynovitis and subcutaneous oedema
Plain radiographs to confirm the absence of erosions
Serum protein electrophoresis and age-appropriate malignancy screening where paraneoplastic disease is suspected
Antinuclear antibodies and thyroid function to exclude mimics
redFlags: Constitutional features such as weight loss, night sweats or lymphadenopathy suggesting occult malignancy
Poor, absent or only transient response to corticosteroids
Rapid relapse on tapering or withdrawal of steroids
Emergence of joint erosions on imaging, pointing to an alternative erosive arthropathy
New neurological, respiratory or systemic symptoms raising concern for a paraneoplastic or overlap disorder
reference.prognosis: The prognosis is generally excellent, with most patients achieving durable remission of a non-erosive arthropathy and being able to withdraw corticosteroids over months. Outcome is less favourable in the paraneoplastic subset, where the course is dictated by the underlying malignancy.
pitfalls: Mislabelling the condition as rheumatoid arthritis and committing the patient to long-term disease-modifying therapy
Failing to screen for occult malignancy in atypical or steroid-refractory cases
Attributing the dorsal oedema to cardiac, renal or venous disease and overlooking the underlying synovitis
Assuming all seronegative polyarthritis in older adults represents this syndrome without confirming the characteristic features
Prematurely stopping corticosteroids and misinterpreting relapse as treatment failure
references: Clinical guidance on seronegative inflammatory arthritis in older adults
management: Low-dose oral corticosteroids are the mainstay and produce a characteristically rapid, often dramatic resolution of the synovitis and dorsal pitting oedema
Taper corticosteroids gradually over months once symptoms settle, aiming for complete withdrawal given the usually self-limiting non-erosive course
NSAIDs and analgesia as adjuncts for symptomatic relief of joint and soft-tissue pain
Hand and foot therapy to maintain function and reduce oedema during the acute inflammatory phase

Undertake age-appropriate malignancy screening, including serum protein electrophoresis, when features are atypical, the steroid response is poor or short-lived, or disease relapses, reflecting the paraneoplastic subset
Monitor for relapse and for evolution into elderly-onset rheumatoid arthritis, reassessing rheumatoid factor and anti-CCP status if the pattern changes
Refer to rheumatology to confirm the diagnosis and guide steroid withdrawal
